learnings.title: Mastering Memoization
learnings.answer:
Chapter 5. Most `useCallback` calls in most codebases prevent nothing. This entry is about why, and about the surprisingly long list of ways memoization silently breaks.

The basics are covered in [useMemo & useCallback](/react-guide/9) and [React.memo and the Reference Trap](/react-guide/15). Start there if comparison-by-reference isn't yet automatic for you.

## Under the hood: the useMemo-vs-useCallback myth

A persistent myth says `useMemo` is cheaper than `useCallback`, because `useCallback` "recreates the function every render."

Half of that is true, and it's true of both.

A hook is just a function React calls on every render. So on every render, the *argument* you pass to it is constructed fresh — that's ordinary JavaScript, nothing to do with React:

```javascript
useCallback(() => submit(data), []);   // this arrow is created every render
useMemo(() => ({ a, b }), [a, b]);     // so is this one
```

The difference is only what happens next:

- **`useCallback`** stores the function it was given and returns the *cached* one, discarding the newly created argument.
- **`useMemo`** calls the function it was given and stores the *return value*.

Both allocate a throwaway function per render. Neither is faster than the other. `useCallback(fn, deps)` is literally `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`.

## Anti-pattern: memoizing props for no reason

```javascript
function Parent() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const onClick = useCallback(() => console.log('click'), []);   // pointless

  return <Child onClick={onClick} />;
}
```

`Child` is not memoized. When `Parent` re-renders, `Child` re-renders — **because its parent re-rendered**, which is the only thing that ever causes a re-render ([entry 1](/advanced-react/1)). Whether `onClick` kept its reference is irrelevant; nobody is comparing it.

All this achieved was extra work for React and a harder-to-read component. And it's never one — they multiply, start depending on each other, and eventually the actual logic is buried under dependency arrays.

**There are exactly two reasons to memoize a prop:**

1. The prop is used as a **dependency of a hook in a downstream component**. An unstable reference there re-triggers that effect on every parent render.
2. The receiving component is wrapped in **`React.memo`**.

If neither applies, don't.

## How `React.memo` actually behaves

When a memoized component's re-render is triggered **by its parent**, React compares props first and skips the render if they're all shallow-equal — stopping the cascade there. If even one prop changed, it re-renders exactly as if `memo` weren't there.

Note the qualifier: *triggered by its parent*. `memo` does nothing about a component's own state updates, and nothing about [context](/advanced-react/8).

## The broken-memoization gallery

`React.memo` only pays off if **every** prop is stable. That's much harder than it sounds. Each of these looks fine and is broken:

**1. An unmemoized prop passed through a middleman**

```javascript
function Middle({ onClick }) {
  return <MemoizedChild onClick={onClick} />;   // Middle isn't memoized...
}

function Parent() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <Middle onClick={() => {}} />;         // ...so this arrow is new every render
}
```

A couple of nesting levels of this and nobody ever spots it.

**2. A function hidden inside a custom hook**

```javascript
function useSubmit() {
  const submit = () => {};      // recreated on every render of the caller
  return { submit };
}

function Parent() {
  const { submit } = useSubmit();
  return <MemoizedChild onSubmit={submit} />;   // broken
}
```

Hooks are functions React calls on every render, so everything declared inside them is rebuilt every render. The instability is real but invisible at the call site.

**3. JSX children**

```javascript
<MemoizedWrapper>
  <Child />
</MemoizedWrapper>
```

Nesting syntax is sugar for `children={<Child />}`. That's a new element object every render, so the prop comparison fails every time. Rewriting it as an explicit prop makes the bug obvious.

**4. Children as a render prop** — same problem, now a new function instead of a new object. See [entry 4](/advanced-react/4).

**5. An element that points at a memoized component**

The subtlest one:

```javascript
const MemoChild = React.memo(Child);

function Parent() {
  return <MemoizedLayout content={<MemoChild />} />;   // still broken
}
```

`<MemoChild />` is an element — a plain object — and *that object* is recreated every render. Memoizing the component does not memoize the element referencing it. You have to memoize the element:

```javascript
const content = useMemo(() => <MemoChild />, []);
return <MemoizedLayout content={content} />;
```

## "Expensive calculations" are rarely the problem

The third common use of `useMemo` is wrapping computations. Ask first: **expensive compared to what?**

Is concatenating strings expensive? Sorting 300 items? A regex over a long document? Nobody knows without measuring — on hardware representative of your users, in the context of everything else happening at that moment.

Sorting a few hundred items takes a couple of milliseconds on a laptop and possibly a hundred times that on an old mid-range phone. A 30ms regex is fine on a settings screen and catastrophic on `mousemove`.

Two things that are reliably true:

- **Rendering usually costs more than the calculation.** Rendering a few hundred list elements typically dwarfs the cost of sorting them. If a list is slow, eliminating unnecessary re-renders beats memoizing the sort.
- **`useMemo` only helps across re-renders.** In a component that never re-renders it does nothing at all — worse than nothing, since the first run still has to populate the cache. One is unmeasurable; hundreds scattered through a large app can measurably slow the initial render.

## Where this is going

The **React Compiler** inserts this memoization automatically at build time, which removes most of the manual work and all of the broken-memoization gallery above. What it cannot do is restructure your tree: [moving state down](/advanced-react/1) and [children as props](/advanced-react/2) remain wins no compiler will perform for you.

## Related

- [Intro to Re-renders](/advanced-react/1) · [Children as Props](/advanced-react/2)
- [Diffing and Reconciliation](/advanced-react/6) — another way to break memoization
- [useMemo & useCallback](/react-guide/9) · [React.memo and the Reference Trap](/react-guide/15)

learnings.title: Diffing, Reconciliation, and the Key Attribute
learnings.answer:
Chapter 6. The *rule* is in [React Guide entry 4](/react-guide/4). This entry is the consequences — which are counter-intuitive enough to look like React malfunctioning.

## The mystery

A form that shows one input for a business tax ID and a different one for a personal tax ID:

```javascript
function Form() {
  const [isBusiness, setIsBusiness] = useState(false);

  return (
    <>
      <Checkbox onChange={() => setIsBusiness((v) => !v)} />
      {isBusiness
        ? <Input id="business-tax-id" placeholder="Business tax ID" />
        : <Input id="personal-tax-id" placeholder="Personal tax ID" />}
    </>
  );
}
```

Type something, flip the checkbox. **The text stays.** Different id, different placeholder, different purpose — and the value you typed survives, as if it's the same field. Which, to React, it is.

## Why: the diff compares by position, then by type

React keeps a tree of plain objects describing what should be on screen. In each object, `type` is either a **string** for a DOM element (`"input"`) or a **reference to the function** for a component.

On a state update, React builds a new tree and compares it with the old one, always at **the same position**:

1. **Same object reference?** Nothing below can have changed — skip the entire subtree. (This is the [children-as-props](/advanced-react/2) bail-out.)
2. **Same `type`?** Reuse the existing instance, update its props. **State is preserved.**
3. **Different `type`?** Unmount the whole old subtree, destroy its instance and everything in it, mount the new one from scratch.

In the form above, both branches produce an element whose `type` is the same `Input` function, at the same position. So React takes path 2: same instance, new props. The `id` and `placeholder` update; the state doesn't.

Flip one branch to a *different* component and you get path 3 instead — unmount, remount, everything lost.

## The anti-pattern this explains: components declared inside components

```javascript
function Form() {
  const [isBusiness, setIsBusiness] = useState(false);

  // A NEW function on every render
  const TaxInput = () => <Input placeholder="Tax ID" />;

  return <TaxInput />;
}
```

`type` here is a reference to `TaxInput` — and that reference changes on every single render, because the function is recreated. React compares old and new, sees different types, and **remounts**.

Remounting is roughly twice as slow as a re-render and produces bizarre symptoms: inputs losing focus mid-keystroke, fields that seemingly can't be typed into, animations restarting, state vanishing. Declare components at module scope, always.

## Fix 1: change the position, not the type

Convert the ternary into two independent conditions:

```javascript
{isBusiness && <Input id="business-tax-id" placeholder="Business tax ID" />}
{!isBusiness && <Input id="personal-tax-id" placeholder="Personal tax ID" />}
```

The children are now an array of three slots instead of two, and React compares slot-by-slot. One slot goes from an element to `null` (unmount), another from `null` to an element (mount). State is destroyed, which is what we wanted.

## Fix 2: give them different keys

```javascript
{isBusiness
  ? <Input key="business" placeholder="Business tax ID" />
  : <Input key="personal" placeholder="Personal tax ID" />}
```

`key` overrides position matching. Different keys mean "these are different things" — unmount one, mount the other.

## What `key` is actually for

In an array, position is unreliable — items reorder, get inserted, get removed. `key` is how React identifies *which item is which* across renders.

**The common misconception is that keys exist for performance — that adding a key prevents list items from re-rendering.** They don't. Keys only establish identity so React reuses the correct instance. Preventing re-renders is `React.memo`'s job, exactly as with any other component.

## Where the two interact: index keys defeat `React.memo`

This is the payoff for understanding both.

Memoize your list items and key them by index:

```javascript
{items.map((item, index) => <MemoRow key={index} item={item} />)}
```

Now reorder the data. The keys stay `0, 1, 2` — they describe position, and position didn't change. But the *data* at each position did. So React matches key `0` to key `0`, compares props, sees `item` changed from one record to another, and re-renders it. Same for every other row. **Every memoized item re-renders.**

Key by identity instead:

```javascript
{items.map((item) => <MemoRow key={item.id} item={item} />)}
```

Now the keys travel with the data. React matches each row to the same record it had before, finds identical props, and skips all of them. Nothing re-renders.

The same holds for insertion: with index keys, prepending one item shifts every subsequent item's props by one, so React re-renders the whole list and mounts one extra at the end. With id keys, the existing rows are untouched and exactly one new row mounts.

## `key` as a state reset

Turn the rule into a tool. To reset a component's internal state when a value changes, key it on that value:

```javascript
<ProfileForm key={userId} userId={userId} />
```

Far more reliable than an effect that calls a pile of setters. It works on any element, not just list items — keying a subtree on the current route resets it on navigation.

One caveat: **this is not really a "state reset."** It forces a full unmount and mount. For a large subtree that's meaningfully more expensive than a re-render, so don't reach for it casually.

## Two quirks worth knowing

**A shared key can force *reuse*.** In Fix 1 above, the two inputs sit in different array slots and don't share state. Give both the *same* key and React concludes it's one element that moved position — and preserves state across the toggle. The exact opposite of Fix 2, from the same mechanism.

**Why React only demands keys for dynamic arrays.** A hand-written list of siblings and a `.map()` produce the same shape. But React can tell them apart: a mapped array arrives as a *nested* array inside the children array. Nesting is the signal that its length and order can change at runtime — a static list can't, so position is a safe identifier and no key is required.

## Related

- [Reconciliation: Diffing by Heuristic](/react-guide/4)
- [Memoization](/advanced-react/5) — why index keys break it
- [Children as Props](/advanced-react/2) — the reference bail-out, step 1 of the diff

learnings.title: Portals: Escaping Overflow and Stacking Contexts
learnings.answer:
Chapter 13. [React Guide entry 24](/react-guide/24) explains what a portal *is*. This entry explains why they had to exist — the answer is entirely CSS. ## The problem A dropdown rendered inside its parent: ```javascript
``` `overflow: hidden` on any ancestor clips the menu. No amount of `position: absolute` or `z-index` escapes it — clipping is applied by the ancestor, and a descendant cannot opt out. The second version of the same problem is stacking contexts. A modal with `z-index: 9999` still renders *behind* a sibling with `z-index: 2` when the modal's ancestor sits in a stacking context of its own. `z-index` only orders elements within their own stacking context, and new contexts are created by more things than most people expect: `position` plus `z-index`, but also `opacity` below 1, `transform`, `filter`, `will-change`, `isolation: isolate`, and `contain`. That last part is what makes this so hard to debug — a `transform` added for an unrelated animation three levels up silently traps everything below it. ## Why the usual fixes fail - **Raising `z-index`** — does nothing across stacking contexts. You can go to `999999` and still lose. - **Removing `overflow: hidden`** — breaks whatever it was there for, usually rounded corners or scroll containment. - **Restructuring the markup** — the menu has to live near its trigger in the component tree for the code to make sense, even though it must live elsewhere in the DOM. That last tension is exactly what a portal resolves. ## The fix ```javascript import { createPortal } from 'react-dom'; function Dropdown({ isOpen, children }) { if (!isOpen) return null; return createPortal(children, document.body); } ``` The DOM node is appended to `document.body`, outside every clipping ancestor and every stacking context. But **in the React tree it's still a child** — which is the part that makes portals useful rather than merely possible: - **Events bubble through the React tree, not the DOM tree.** A click inside the portal fires handlers on its React ancestors, even though the DOM node is elsewhere. Usually what you want; occasionally surprising, since an outside-click handler on the parent will *not* treat the portal as "outside". - **Context works normally.** Theme, locale, and store providers reach into the portal. - **State and lifecycle are unchanged.** It mounts and unmounts with its React parent. ## What a portal does not do for you A portal solves layout, not accessibility or positioning: - **Position it yourself.** Detached from its trigger in the DOM, it no longer follows on scroll or resize. Measure the trigger and position the portal ([entry 12](/advanced-react/12)), and update on scroll. - **Focus management is manual.** Move focus in on open, trap it while open, restore it to the trigger on close, close on Escape. - **Announce it properly** — `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"`, and a label. - **Rendering into `document.body` directly can conflict** with other libraries doing the same. A dedicated `
` is tidier. For anything beyond a simple case, a headless library (Radix, React Aria, Floating UI) has already solved positioning, collision detection, and focus management correctly. ## Related - [Portals](/react-guide/24) · [MCQ Hit-List: CSS](/test-prep/19) — stacking contexts - [Escaping Flickering UI with useLayoutEffect](/advanced-react/12) — positioning the portal - [Accessibility in React](/react-learnings/18)

learnings.title: Data Fetching and Performance: Request Waterfalls
learnings.answer:
Chapter 14. The single biggest performance problem in data-driven React apps, and one this app didn't cover at all before now.

## What a waterfall is

Requests that *could* run in parallel end up running in sequence, so total time is their sum rather than their maximum.

```javascript
function Page() {
  const user = useUser();                    // starts immediately
  const permissions = usePermissions(user);  // waits for user
  const projects = useProjects(user);        // waits for user

  if (!user) return <Spinner />;
  return <Dashboard ... />;
}
```

Three 300ms requests take 900ms instead of 300ms — and only `permissions` genuinely needed `user` first.

## Waterfall 1: nested components each fetching

The most common cause, and the hardest to see because each component looks reasonable on its own.

```javascript
function Page() {
  const { data: user, loading } = useFetch('/api/user');
  if (loading) return <Spinner />;
  return <Sidebar userId={user.id} />;   // Sidebar only mounts now
}

function Sidebar({ userId }) {
  const { data, loading } = useFetch(`/api/projects/${userId}`);   // starts LATE
  if (loading) return <Spinner />;
  return <ProjectList projects={data} />;
}
```

`Sidebar` doesn't exist until `Page` finishes, so its request can't start until then. Add a third level and you have three sequential round trips before anything renders. **Each early return on a loading state creates a barrier that blocks every request below it.**

## Waterfall 2: awaiting sequentially

```javascript
// BAD — 900ms
const user = await fetchUser();
const settings = await fetchSettings();
const notifications = await fetchNotifications();

// GOOD — 300ms
const [user, settings, notifications] = await Promise.all([
  fetchUser(),
  fetchSettings(),
  fetchNotifications(),
]);
```

Only `await` in sequence when a request genuinely needs the previous result. When some do and some don't, start the independent ones first:

```javascript
const settingsPromise = fetchSettings();          // fired now, not awaited
const user = await fetchUser();
const permissions = await fetchPermissions(user.id);
const settings = await settingsPromise;           // already in flight
```

## The three strategies

| Strategy | What happens | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Fetch-on-render** | Component mounts, then requests. The default with `useEffect`. | Every level of nesting adds a round trip |
| **Fetch-then-render** | Fetch everything up front, render when it's all done | No waterfall, but the slowest request gates the whole page |
| **Render-as-you-fetch** | Start requests *before* rendering, render each part as its data lands | Fastest, needs a router or cache layer to kick requests off early |

The route to the third one is starting requests outside the component tree — a route loader, a cache prefetch, or a server component that begins fetching before the client renders anything.

## Practical fixes

**Hoist the fetches.** Request everything the page needs at the top and pass data down. Ugly, but it collapses N round trips into one.

**Prefetch on intent.** Start the request when the user hovers a link or focuses a control:

```javascript
<Link onMouseEnter={() => queryClient.prefetchQuery(['project', id], fetchProject)} />
```

By the time the click registers, the data is often already there.

**Don't block on every loading state.** Render the shell, and let each region show its own spinner. Suspense expresses this well:

```javascript
<Suspense fallback={<PageSkeleton />}>
  <Header />
  <Suspense fallback={<SidebarSkeleton />}>
    <Sidebar />
  </Suspense>
</Suspense>
```

Note that `Suspense` here is doing something different from [code-splitting](/react-guide/17): with `use()` or a Suspense-capable data library it suspends on **data**, not on a module download.

**Use a cache library.** React Query, SWR, and RTK Query deduplicate identical in-flight requests, cache across components, and expose prefetching. Two components asking for the same user fire one request.

**Move it to the server.** A React Server Component fetches on the server, where the data is a few milliseconds away rather than a network round trip — nested awaits there are far cheaper.

## How to spot one

Open the Network tab and look at the waterfall chart. Requests that start in a staircase — each beginning as the previous ends — are the bug. Requests that start together are fine.

## Related

- [Data Fetching and Race Conditions](/advanced-react/15)
- [Server State vs. Client State](/react-guide/27) · [Code-Splitting with lazy + Suspense](/react-guide/17)
- [RSC, Actions & use()](/react-guide/30)

learnings.title: Universal Error Handling in React
learnings.answer:
Chapter 16. [Error Boundaries](/react-guide/25) covers what they catch. This entry is about the much larger set of errors they **don't**, and what to do about those. ## What boundaries actually catch An error boundary catches errors thrown during **rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors** of the tree below it. ```javascript class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component { state = { error: null }; static getDerivedStateFromError(error) { return { error }; // render the fallback } componentDidCatch(error, info) { logToService(error, info.componentStack); // report it } render() { if (this.state.error) return this.props.fallback; return this.props.children; } } ``` There is still no hook equivalent — a class is required, or `react-error-boundary`, which wraps one. ## What they miss This is the important list: | Not caught | Why | |---|---| | **Event handlers** | Run outside rendering — React isn't on the stack | | **Async code** (`setTimeout`, promises, `fetch` callbacks) | The stack has unwound; the throw happens later | | **Server-side rendering** | Boundaries don't operate during SSR | | **Errors in the boundary itself** | It can't catch its own render error | In practice most real errors are in that column. A failed fetch, a bad click handler, a rejected mutation — none of them reach a boundary. ## Getting async errors into a boundary The trick is to convert an async failure into a **render-time** error by routing it through state: ```javascript function useErrorHandler() { const [error, setError] = useState(null); if (error) throw error; // thrown during render — the boundary sees it return setError; } function Profile() { const throwError = useErrorHandler(); useEffect(() => { fetchProfile().catch(throwError); // async failure becomes a render error }, [throwError]); } ``` `react-error-boundary` ships this as `useErrorBoundary`. Use it deliberately. Not every failed request should blow away a subtree — a failed search deserves an inline message, while a failed "load the thing this page is about" deserves the boundary. ## Boundary placement One boundary at the root turns any error into a blank page. Instead, place them where a failure has a natural containment: ```javascript }> {/* last resort */} }> {/* one widget dies alone */} }> ``` Rule of thumb: a boundary belongs wherever you can answer *"what should the user see if just this part fails?"* ## Reset and retry A boundary that latches into its error state forever is a dead subtree. Give it a way back: ```javascript (

{error.message}

)} onReset={() => refetch()} resetKeys={[userId]} // auto-reset when this changes > ``` `resetKeys` is the important one — without it, an error on one profile persists after navigating to a different profile, because the boundary has no idea the context changed. ## Composing with Suspense Boundaries and `Suspense` are complementary: `Suspense` handles "not ready yet", the boundary handles "it failed". Order matters — the boundary goes outside: ```javascript }> }> ``` ## The layers you actually need Boundaries are one of five, and alone they're not enough: 1. **Error boundaries** — render-time failures 2. **`try/catch` in event handlers and async functions** — the majority of real errors 3. **Per-request error states** — a failed fetch usually deserves inline UI plus retry, not a boundary 4. **A global `window.onerror` / `unhandledrejection` listener** — the safety net for everything that escaped 5. **Reporting** — `componentDidCatch` sends the component stack somewhere you'll actually see it ```javascript window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', (event) => { logToService(event.reason); }); ``` ## Related - [Error Boundaries](/react-guide/25) - [Data Fetching and Race Conditions](/advanced-react/15) - [Code-Splitting with lazy + Suspense](/react-guide/17)
